subject: Cooking
title: Eggs Don't Raise Your Cholesterol
description: A fast breakdown of Eggs Don't Raise Your Cholesterol for builders.

hook.text: For 40 years, eggs were demonized. 'Limit to 3 per week,' doctors said. That advice was wrong.

buildup.text: Eggs contain 186mg of cholesterol. So logically, eating them should raise blood cholesterol — right?

discovery.text: Your liver produces 1,000–2,000mg of cholesterol daily. When you eat more, your liver simply makes less.

twist.text: Saturated fat — not dietary cholesterol — is the main driver of elevated blood cholesterol for most people.

climax.text: In 2015, the USDA removed cholesterol limits from dietary guidelines, effectively rehabilitating the egg.

punchline.text: Eggs were innocent. The real villain was always saturated fat.

quiz.question: What did the 2015 USDA dietary guidelines change about cholesterol?
options: Removed the daily cholesterol limit entirely

details.summary: Decades of research have shown that dietary cholesterol from eggs has minimal impact on blood cholesterol for most people. The body compensates by reducing its own cholesterol production. Eggs are now considered a nutritious, affordable protein source by major health organizations.
details.whyItMatters: The egg-cholesterol myth caused millions of people to avoid one of nature's most nutritious foods for decades. Updated dietary guidelines now reflect the science exonerating eggs.
takeaways: Dietary cholesterol has modest effect on blood cholesterol levels
The body reduces its own production when dietary intake increases
Current guidelines removed the daily cholesterol limit of 300 mg

faq.question: How many eggs per day are considered safe?
faq.answer: Most research supports 1 to 3 eggs daily as safe for healthy adults with no increased cardiovascular risk. Some studies show no harm from even higher consumption. People with specific genetic conditions affecting cholesterol metabolism should consult their doctor.

faq.question: Why were eggs wrongly blamed for decades?
faq.answer: Early research in the 1960s linked dietary cholesterol to heart disease. Eggs are high in cholesterol, so they were restricted. Better studies later showed saturated and trans fats affect blood cholesterol far more than dietary cholesterol. The 2015 Dietary Guidelines removed the cholesterol cap.
